en: in; at; to (a place or a time)
note: 서울에 가요, 세 시에 만나요, 집에 있어요. Static location and destination.
Where an action happens – 식당에서 먹어요 – and where you came from: 영국에서 왔어요. Contrast with 에, which is for being somewhere.

en: the politeness tag on the end of a sentence
note: Add 요 and you're polite; strip it and you're in banmal. It even props up bare words: 저요? 여기요, 조금만요.
Pushes out 은/는 and 이/가 rather than stacking: 저도요 'me too'.
친구한테 말했어요. 에게 in writing, 께 when the person outranks you: 선생님께.
거 is the spoken form: 이거, 그거, 제 거.
가고 싶어요 'I'd like to go', 먹고 싶어요. For wanting a thing, use …이/가 필요해요 or just …주세요.

en: commands and requests at three politeness levels
note: 앉으세요 is your everyday polite request; 앉아 is banmal; 앉으십시오 belongs to signs and announcements. Add 주세요 to ask a favour: 도와주세요.
The default apology to strangers and for anything that matters. 죄송해요 is a shade softer.
저는 앤이에요. 제 이름은 …예요 is the fuller version.
The spoken workhorse, from 그런데. 하지만 belongs to writing.
Korean runs two number systems. Native numbers count things, people and hours – 한 개, 한 명, 한 시. Sino numbers (일, 이, 삼 …) do money, dates, minutes and phone numbers.
두 개, 두 명이요 'a table for two', 두 시. Sino form 이.
세 개, 세 시. Sino form 삼.
네 개, 네 시. Sino form 사 – which sounds like the word for death, so some lifts label the 4th floor F.

en: older sister – 누나 if you're male, 언니 if you're female
note: Younger sister is 여동생. These four terms are also used for close non-relatives slightly older than you.
Reliably produces delight and then a torrent of fast Korean.
A rising 네? on its own does the same job.

en: soup – the bowl that comes with the rice
note: 찌개 is the thicker, spicier stew: 김치찌개, 된장찌개.
Also 'hold that thought' and 'stop right there'.
Point and say it. Swap in any number: 두 개 주세요.
영국 사람이에요 'I'm British'. Expect 어! 영국! and a comment about football.
이게 = 이것이 with the subject particle. Dropping it gives 이거 뭐예요?, which is what people actually say.
The pointing-at-the-menu line. 이걸로 할게요 'I'll go with this one'.

en: the honorific infix for the person you're speaking about
note: Hidden inside 하세요, 가세요, 앉으세요. Special forms: 드시다 (eat/drink), 계시다 (be), 주무시다 (sleep), 말씀하시다 (speak). Never use it about yourself.
Same three-way split as the present: ㅏ/ㅗ stems take 았 (갔어요), the rest take 었 (먹었어요), 하다 gives 했어요. No object agreement and no ergative marker to worry about.
진짜 also works as 'really, very': 진짜 맛있어요. 정말 is its tidier twin.
replaces WhatsApp entirely in Korea; everyone says 카톡. 카톡 해요 = message me
the polite command and the family nudge in one ending; contrast with -아/어 주세요 (do it FOR me). Never use it about yourself

en: word order: the verb always lands last
note: Korean is subject-object-verb, and the particles (은/는, 이/가, 을/를) do the job English does with position. Anything obvious is simply dropped: 어디 가요?, 먹었어요?
제 가방 is 저의 contracted. Spoken Korean often just stacks the nouns: 친구 집 'my friend's place'.
버스로 가요 'by bus', 오른쪽으로 'to the right'. 'From a place' is 에서, 'from a time' is 부터.
Close friends, children and juniors only. 네가 as subject, said 'niga' so it isn't heard as 내가.
The banmal answer to 네. Using it upwards is rude – worth recognising more than saying.

en: to talk; to tell someone about something
note: 얘기해요; full form 이야기하다.
Hang 는요? off the person's name: 민수 씨는요? Never 당신은요?
-아/어야 돼요 is the general 'have to': 지금 가야 돼요.
Between nouns, use 나/이나 instead: 커피나 차.
Korean puts the reason first and glues it on: 늦어서 죄송해요 'sorry I'm late'. 왜냐하면 is stiff and rare in speech.
All-purpose: surprise, sympathy, and the noise Koreans make standing up.

en: auntie – what you call the woman running a restaurant
note: Literally 'mum's sister'. 이모님! is how regulars call the server over; warmer than 저기요.

en: boss – how you address any shop or restaurant owner
note: Safe and slightly flattering for whoever is behind the counter, man or woman – 사장님 carries no gender. 기사님 for a driver, 선생님 when you're unsure.
갈 수 있어요 'I can go'. The quick spoken negative is 못: 못 가요 'I can't go'.
아줌마 is the casual clip, and can sting if she thinks she's too young for it.
남자 친구 = boyfriend. 소년 'boy' is literary.
여자 친구 = girlfriend.
Never used face to face.
Same syllable as 차 'tea'; context does the work. 택시 for a taxi.
캐리어 for a wheeled suitcase.
What the host or server says. The guest's line is 잘 먹겠습니다 before eating, 잘 먹었습니다 after.
어느 나라 사람이에요? is the plainer version.
The standard Korean invitation to sit and talk.
돼지고기 pork, 소고기 beef, 닭고기 chicken. 고기 빼 주세요 'no meat, please'.
From -지요. 맛있죠? 'lovely, isn't it?'; 그렇죠 'exactly'.
Sometimes met with an amused 'it's not spicy' as the sweat starts.
밥 먹고 있어요 'I'm eating'. Plain 해요 already covers most English -ing, so save this for things happening at this moment.

en: to let someone know; to tell
note: 알려주세요 'do let me know'.
가지 마세요 'don't go', 걱정하지 마세요 'don't worry'.
시간 있으면 'if you've got time', 도착하면 'when I arrive'.
뜻 = meaning. The 'I mean…' filler is 그니까 / 그러니까.

en: adjectives take a special form in front of a noun
note: 좋다 → 좋은 사람 'a good person', but 사람이 좋아요 'the person is nice'. Korean adjectives are verbs, so there's no gender or number to agree with.
다음에 또 뵐게요 is the politer version.
서울역까지 가 주세요 'to Seoul Station, please'. Pairs with 부터: 아홉 시부터 여섯 시까지.
갈 거예요 'I'll go'. For an on-the-spot promise use -(으)ㄹ게요 instead: 갈게요 'right, I'm off'.
갈까요? 'shall we go?'; 제가 할까요? 'shall I do it?'; 뭐 먹을까요? 'what shall we eat?'
맛있는 것 같아요 'I think it's nice'. Koreans hedge with 같아요 far more than English speakers do, and a flat opinion can sound abrupt without it.
The soft way to leave; 먼저 가 볼게요 if others are staying.
-주시겠어요? is the extra-polite ask. Everyday version: 물 좀 주세요.
Cheap, metered and everywhere, hailed by hand or through the 카카오 T app. Nothing is ever negotiated.
표 for transport, 티켓 for events.
Part of the name itself: 서울역, 강남역, 홍대입구역.
편의점 is the convenience store on every corner, open all night.
당연하죠 is the more emphatic 'obviously'.
갈 때 'when you go', 어릴 때 'when I was little'.
밖에 = outside, and also 'except', as in 이것밖에 없어요 'this is all there is'.
보여 주세요 = show me, please
a KakaoTalk message is a 카톡

en: 'my … hurts' frame: 머리가 아파요, 배가 아파요
note: the body part is the subject, not you. Illnesses use different frames: 열이 나요, 감기에 걸렸어요

en: how much does it come to altogether?

note: the taxi line; 내려 주세요 also works
later the same day; 나중에 봐요 for some other time
전화번호 = phone number
rent is 월세, not this
달걀 is the same thing
김치찌개, 된장찌개 – the everyday hot dish at almost any meal
the standard polite refusal of more food or help – 괜찮아요 alone does the job
native 열하나 for counting things
native 열둘
written 십육 but said simnyuk
native 예순
native 일흔
native 여든
native 아흔
아빠 = dad, used well into adulthood
남동생 = younger brother; 동생 alone when the sex is obvious
삼겹살 (pork belly) is the default barbecue; 소고기 = beef
the counter for drinks is 잔, not 컵
젓가락 = chopsticks; the pair together is 수저. Rice and soup are eaten with the spoon
불 켜다 / 불 끄다 – the same word also means fire
에게 is the written form of 한테
full form 어디에서
랑 after a vowel, 이랑 after a consonant; 하고 and 와/과 are the neutral and written versions
the spoken intensifier – 완전 맛있어요. 완전히 is the proper adverb
for places rather than goods, use … 어디 있어요?
said while showing the address on your phone; taxis are metered, so there is nothing to negotiate
좀 is the softener that makes a request polite rather than blunt
slangy but universal; 진짜요? for a plainer 'really?'
조심히 가세요 = mind how you go – said at nearly every goodbye

en: shoes off before you go in
note: applies in homes, guesthouses, temples and any floor-seating restaurant

en: can I take this away, please
note: Say '포장이요' at the counter; 여기서 먹을게요 = eating in.
KakaoTalk is the WhatsApp of Korea; 카톡 is the everyday clipping.
Note the subject particle, not an object: 시간이 필요해요.
Also what you say through the door.
Hours take native numbers (한, 두, 세), 반 = half.
Minutes take Sino numbers, so the two systems meet inside one clock time.
Spicy by default. 라멘 is the Japanese kind, a different dish.
찌개 = thick stew; the other two you'll see everywhere are 된장찌개 and 순두부찌개.
The default savoury street snack; sold with 순대 and 튀김.

en: shall I heat it up for you?
note: Asked at every convenience store; answer 네, 데워 주세요.
Korean ones are flat metal. 수저 = the spoon-and-chopsticks set.
Green cross sign; pharmacists speak some English in cities.
What the doctor asks you, in the 세요 honorific.
Back it up with 못 먹어요 (I can't eat it); allergy labelling is patchy.
병원 covers any clinic, so 'go to hospital' is said for a sore throat too.
Adjective + 거 makes 'the ... one': 큰 거, 매운 거, 이거 말고 저거.
저의 shrinks to 제, 나의 to 내. Spoken Korean usually drops it: 친구 집 = my friend's place.
Contraction of 이것을; likewise 그걸, 저걸, 뭘.

en: the four-way grid: 이거-그거-저거-어느 거, 여기-거기-저기-어디, 이렇게-그렇게-저렇게-어떻게
note: 이 = near me, 그 = near you or already mentioned, 저 = away from both of us. The 그 row does the work English 'it' and 'that' do.
The default hedge. Koreans soften opinions with it constantly: 맛있는 것 같아요.
대박 is the everyday 'no way / amazing'.

en: go in order to do: 밥 먹으러 가요, 보러 왔어요
note: Attaches to the verb stem and pairs with 가다/오다/다니다.
여기서 멀어요? = is it far from here?
-아/어도 돼요? = may I. Careful with 자리 있어요?, which literally asks 'is there a seat?': at a restaurant door it means 'have you got a table free?', so 네 means yes, come in.
현금영수증? = 'cash receipt?' is asked at every till; just say 괜찮아요.
T머니, bought in any convenience store; tap for subway, bus and even taxis. 카카오페이 covers phone payments.

en: could you put the aircon on

note: Works for good news and bad; 진짜? = really?

en: take me to this address, please
note: Korean taxis always run the meter, so there is nothing to agree in advance. Show the address on your phone and say this.
A host's offer. Staff say 뭐 드릴까요? or 주문하시겠어요?

en: stay and eat before you go
note: The classic Korean host line, and often just a warm goodbye rather than a literal offer.

word: 덥다 → 더워요 / 듣다 → 들어요 / 모르다 → 몰라요
roman: deopda → deowoyo / deutda → deureoyo / moreuda → mollayo
en: irregular stems: the verbs that change shape before 아/어요
note: ㅂ→우 (맵다 매워요, 춥다 추워요), ㄷ→ㄹ (걷다 걸어요), ㅡ drops (바쁘다 바빠요, 쓰다 써요), 르→ㄹㄹ (빠르다 빨라요), ㅅ drops (낫다 나아요). Five patterns cover nearly every verb you meet.
갈게요 'right, I'm off', 이걸로 할게요 'I'll take this one', 계산할게요 'I'll pay'. Only ever about yourself, and only as a response to the other person; a plain plan is -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

en: …, isn't it – reacting to what's in front of you
note: 맛있네요, 비싸네요, 한국말 잘하시네요. Marks something you have just noticed, and it is how compliments and small talk are actually made: 날씨 좋네요.

en: the 합니다 level: 갑니다, 먹습니다, 감사합니다
note: Vowel stem + ㅂ니다 (갑니다), consonant stem + 습니다 (먹습니다); questions take -ㅂ니까?/-습니까?. Mostly a recognition skill – staff, announcements and the news aim it at you all day.
The first thing a café or fast-food till asks. Answer 여기서 먹을게요 or 포장이요.
Called out by every shop, café and restaurant as you walk in. Nothing is expected back; a nod is plenty.

en: right, tucking in / that was lovely, thank you
note: Said before and after any meal someone else has cooked or paid for. The 합니다 form is standard here even among friends.

en: not at all; don't mention it
note: Reply to thanks. 아니에요 and 괜찮아요 do the same job and are heard more.
Meals are 아침 (breakfast), 점심 (lunch), 저녁 (dinner).
마음에 들어요 – used of something you've just been shown or given.
On the phone: 저 앤인데요.
건강하세요 'keep well' is the version for older people.
도움이 필요해요 'I need some help'.
Banmal only – friends and juniors. Rude in every other direction. To flag down a stranger, use 저기요.
Turns a clause into a noun: 한국어 배우는 게 재미있어요 'learning Korean is fun'.
Spoken squeeze of 그렇죠 – a nudge for agreement.
The formal register of 고마워요; interchangeable with 감사합니다 in practice.
For someone you know, not a greeting for strangers.
제 거예요 'it's mine'; 누구 거예요? 'whose is this?'
밥 먹은 후에. 먹고 나서 is the spoken version.
가기 전에 'before going'.
한 번도 안 가 봤어요 'I've never been'.
Korean doubles the negative: 아무것도 안 했어요 'I did nothing'.
준비됐어요?
몸이 안 좋아요 'I'm not feeling well'.

en: are you unwell?; where does it hurt?

note: 비 와요 'it's raining'; 장마 is the summer rainy season.
Written 네 but said 니, to keep it clear of 내 'my' and 네 'yes'.
The base flavour of most spicy Korean food. 된장 soybean paste, 참기름 sesame oil, 간장 soy sauce.
채식주의자예요 'I'm vegetarian', though 고기 빼 주세요 'no meat, please' is what actually gets results – and watch for 멸치 (anchovy) stock in almost everything.
operating a device is 켜다, not this
usually said 티비
더러워요
hotel key card is 카드키
최고예요! – warm, everyday praise
in speech people just say 머리가 아파요
The everyday non-meat protein: 순두부 (silken, in stew), 부침 두부 (firm, pan-fried).
누구 거예요? = whose is this?
아래에 is the same thing, slightly more formal
앞에 = in front of
외- marks the mother's side: 외할머니, 외할아버지, 외삼촌. The father's side takes 친- or no prefix at all.
The signature finishing oil, drizzled on at the end rather than cooked in.
고추장 = chilli paste, 고춧가루 = chilli flakes
Korean menus have no veg/non-veg split – you name what to leave out. Watch for 멸치 (anchovy) stock in almost everything
convenience stores ask 데워 드릴까요? = shall I warm it up for you?

en: shall I get you a coffee?
note: the host's offer – coffee, not tea, is the Korean default
시원한 물 = chilled water; 물 셀프 on a sign means help yourself
이불 = the duvet/bedding; guesthouses and older homes often use floor bedding
what restaurants and cafés say

en: put it in the fridge, please

note: 무슨 색이에요? = what colour is it?
Korean avoids saying 'you' – use the person's name + 씨, or their title + 님 (선생님, 사장님)
그러고 나서 for a stronger 'and then'

en: roughly what will it come to?
note: asking the likely fare, not haggling over it
값 is the more spoken word
통화 중 = on the phone / engaged
The opener that buys you a second before you make your point; 그니까 and 근데 do the same job.
the phone-call filler that keeps a chat moving
present is -고 있어요 (뭐 하고 있어요?)
Korean has no fused fraction words like डेढ़ – just 반 'half' added on
attaches directly: 세 시쯤, 만 원쯤

en: I'm going to be a bit late
note: -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 is the standard hedge; saying things flat sounds abrupt
unrelated middle-aged men are 아저씨, never 삼촌

en: uncle and aunt terms encode which parent's sibling it is: 고모 father's sister, 이모 mother's sister
note: 이모 doubles as the friendly word for the woman running a small restaurant – you will hear it constantly
화났어요
여기서 내려 주세요
softens bad news or a refusal
the 합니다-level greeting – announcements, officials, a first meeting with someone senior. 안녕하세요 is the everyday default

en: could you drive a bit slower

note: 차가 막혀요 = the traffic's bad; 교통카드 = the travel card you tap on every bus and train
약국 = pharmacy, marked with a green cross
no word for 'quarter' – 세 시 십오 분 = quarter past three
also 현금인출기; every convenience store has one
112 for police, 119 for fire and ambulance
Shoes come off in homes, guesthouses, temples and floor-seating restaurants, so your socks are on show. Pack a decent pair.
땅콩 알레르기 있어요 = I'm allergic to peanuts
What staff call after you as you leave a shop.
한국 사람처럼 = like a Korean. 같이 works the same way.
After a noun. After a verb use -아/어서.
The standard reply to 잘 지내요? when things are just okay.
Lives in 재미있어요 (it's fun/interesting) and 재미없어요.
Native numbers count things, people and hours; before a counter it shortens to 스물한 개, 스물한 살.
Sino numbers do money, minutes, dates, floors and phone numbers. Learn both sets in parallel.
며칠 asks the day of the month; 무슨 요일이에요? asks the weekday.

en: polite warm address to a woman serving you
note: Standard in restaurants; 사장님 works everywhere if you're unsure.
얼음 빼 주세요 = no ice, please. Cafes default to iced (아이스).
쌈 = wrapping a piece of grilled meat in a leaf; the raw-leaf plate that arrives with barbecue.
Often served raw to grill alongside meat.
The everyday aromatic. Coriander (고수) is rare in Korean food, unlike in Hindi cooking.
고춧가루 = chilli powder, 소금 = salt.
The free tea-water on the table; 물은 셀프 means help yourself to water.
False friend: it is clear fizzy lemonade, never alcoholic cider. 콜라 = cola.
무슨 맛이에요? = what does it taste of / which flavour is it?
In practice say 고기 안 먹어요 (I don't eat meat) and check for 멸치/젓갈 stock, which is in almost everything.
Meat at the table is cut with 가위, scissors.
The verb inside 비빔밥; 섞다 is the general 'mix'.

en: how many portions would you like?
note: 인분 = portions per person; meat and stews are ordered this way, minimum two.
The one appliance in every Korean kitchen; it cooks the rice and keeps it warm all day.
Homes are floor-heated (온돌), so people sit and sleep on the 바닥.
The sunken bit inside the front door; shoes never go past it.
Korean summers are full of them; 모기약 = repellent.
치약 = toothpaste. Many Koreans brush at work after lunch.
Sorting is compulsory: 음식물 (food), 재활용 (recycling), 일반 (general).
Street bins are scarce, so people carry rubbish home.
From 'concent', not English 'consent'. Korea uses 220V round two-pin. 스위치 = switch.

en: could you put the heating on
note: The boiler runs both the underfloor heating and the hot water; 온수 = hot water setting.
허리가 아파요 is one of the most common complaints you'll hear.
부터 = from, 까지 = until.
Native day-words: 하루, 이틀, 사흘.

en: could I have something for a fever
note: 진통제 = painkiller, 소화제 = for indigestion, 감기약 = cold medicine.
한테 = to a person, 한테서 = from a person; 에게(서) is the written form.
저한테 is the polite pair. Choosing 나 or 저 sets your whole register.
그분한테서 is the honorific version.
(으)로 alone also means 'towards': 어디로 가세요?
아니면 = or, or else.
전혀 always needs a negative after it; 별로요 = not really.
엄청 and 진짜 are the spoken intensifiers; 매우 is textbook-only.
지금 나가요 = I'm heading out now.
The Uber of Korea, in the 카카오T app; it also books trains and hire bikes.
연착됐어요 is the announcement word. Korean trains are famously punctual, so you'll use this about buses.
지금 가고 있어요 works too.
Short for 단체 카톡방; where Korean social life is organised.
보조배터리 = power bank.
통화 = a phone conversation.
Young and very spoken. 어머 is the older women's version, 아이고 the all-purpose one.
-네요 marks something you've just noticed; softer praise than 좋아요.
Dial 119 for ambulance and fire, 112 for police.
Signs and manuals. In speech use 쓰다.
공 is what you say in phone numbers: 공일공 = 010.
Money is spoken in 만 units: 15,000 won is 만 오천 원.

en: dates: Sino number + 월, Sino number + 일
note: Big to small, year then month then day. Watch 유월 (not 육월) and 시월 (not 십월).
Korean months are simply number + 월, so all twelve cost you one rule.
Irregular: 육월 is wrong.
Irregular: 십월 is wrong.
Runs the underfloor heating (온돌) as well as the taps.
Said to elders in the morning; 잘 잤어요? between equals. 좋은 아침 is a translation nobody really uses.
Asked as 무슨 일 하세요?, not 직업이 뭐예요? which sounds like a form.
병원 covers hospital and clinic alike, so 응급실 is the A&E department inside it. Dial 119 for an ambulance, 112 for police.
Pour with two hands for anyone older, and never top up your own glass.

en: about to, intending to: 나가려고 해요
note: For 'just this second about to', use 막 나가려던 참이에요.

en: let me know when you get there
note: 연락 주세요 = get in touch; -(으)면 = when/if.
Shoes come off at the door of homes, many guesthouses and some restaurants; 실내화 = indoor shoes.
안경 쓰다 = to wear glasses, the same 쓰다 again.

en: the long negative: 가지 않아요 = I don't go
note: Same meaning as 안 가요, but commoner in writing and careful speech. 맛없다 and 재미없다 are their own words, not built with this.
Sino numbers: 삼 층, 몇 층이에요?, 지하 일 층 for the basement. Korean bars and restaurants stack up buildings, so the floor is part of the address.
The default Korean coffee, iced all year round: 아이스 아메리카노, clipped to 아아. 따아 is the hot one; 라떼 is the other staple.
건배! or 위하여!. Hold your glass lower than an elder's, turn away for the first sip, and never fill your own.
미세먼지 심해요 'the air's bad today'. Checked on the phone like the forecast, and the stock spring complaint.

en: I look forward to it; please be good to me
note: Closes any first introduction, straight after 만나서 반갑습니다. There is no English equivalent; it is simply what you say.
Opens a question to a stranger: 실례지만 여기가 어디예요? 저기요 gets their attention first; 실례합니다 is for squeezing past.
The first thing said to a British visitor, usually with 손흥민 and 토트넘 attached. 야구 fills the stadiums; 경기 = a match.

en: this stop is …, doors open on the right
note: The subway announcement, in 합니다 style and repeated in English after the Korean. 다음 역 = the next stop, 환승 = change here.

en: have you got an English menu?
note: Outside tourist areas menus are Korean-only with no pictures. 사진 있어요? 'any photos?' is the fallback, and pointing at the next table works too.
only works at traditional markets – shops and chains have fixed prices
markets often sell by the 근 (600 g)
rarely needed – Korea is close to cashless, card and phone pay everywhere
설거지하다 = to do the dishes
stiff in speech – everyday 'for me' is carried by -아/어 주세요 instead
Korean avoids third-person pronouns – name the person or their role instead. 그분 is the polite 'that person'
Korean rarely marks the habitual past. Plain past plus 예전에 ('back then') covers it: 예전에 자주 갔어요.
생신 is the honorific of 생일 – used for grandparents, parents-in-law and bosses
Cards and phone payments dominate, so change rarely comes up at all.
announcements say O번 승강장; 플랫폼 is also understood
worn at 명절 and weddings; rental shops near the palaces get you in free
설탕 없이 = without sugar; for food orders 빼고 (leaving out) is more natural: 고수 빼고요.
Spoken Korean usually just uses 어디: 어디 갔어요? For 'anywhere', see 아무 데나.

en: how many children do you have?
note: 명 is the counter for people.
The cabbage kimchi is made from; 양배추 is the round European cabbage.
A stock side dish and the base of 콩나물국, the hangover soup.
The nice kind of heat, unlike flat 맵다. 짜다 = salty, 달다 = sweet.
The 합니다 register you hear from staff and on TV; your everyday form stays 맛있어요.
덜 익었어요. Raw fish is 회 and is deliberate, not undercooked.
Every restaurant has a 정수기 and self-serve cups; tap water is drinkable but nobody drinks it.
반찬통 = side-dish tub.
In flat listings you'll see 방 (room) counted instead: 투룸 = two rooms.
천장 = the ceiling inside.
Korean doors take a 비밀번호 (code) rather than a key.
빗자루 is a broom, but the hoover is the everyday tool.
빨래 = laundry, 세탁소 = the dry cleaner's.

en: did you turn the gas off?
note: Gas is 잠그다 (shut off), not 끄다.
The emotional heart is 마음.

en: to have no energy, feel weak
note: 기운이 없어요. 약하다 describes a weak thing, not a poorly person.
핑크색 is just as common in speech; -색 = colour.
Blunt and best avoided about people; 통통하다 is the softer 'chubby'.
께 replaces 한테 for real deference: 부모님께.
우리 집, 친구 집; 댁 is the honorific house: 부모님 댁.
보다 is the comparison particle: 이게 저것보다 싸요. 덜 = less.
바꾸다 = to swap; the standard 'pass me to' on the phone.
기본요금 = the starting fare; the meter always runs, no negotiating.

en: could you do it a bit cheaper
note: Only at traditional markets. Shops, cafes and chains have fixed prices and haggling is rude.
소리가 안 들려요 = I can't hear you.
괜찮아요 does most of the consoling work in Korean.
Temple names end in -사: 불국사. The same word 절 also means a bow.
Korean has no 'quarter to' word: 여섯 시 십오 분 전, or just say 다섯 시 사십오 분.
저기서 오른쪽으로 도세요. Signs use 우회전 (right turn) and 좌회전 (left turn).
Korean relative clauses go in front of the noun: 밥 먹는 곳 = a place to eat.

en: nothing to be done about it
note: The resigned shrug; 할 수 없죠 works the same.
Very common in men's speech; 아내 is the neutral word and 집사람 the old-fashioned one.
Markets sell meat and veg by the 근; shops use kilos and grams.
봉투 (carrier bag) is chargeable at every shop, so bring your own.
야구 fills the stadiums; 축구 is what you'll be asked about, usually with 손흥민 in the same breath.
무릎이 아파요, a stock complaint after all that hill walking.
